what_it_does: Transient execution vulnerabilities (like Spectre and Meltdown) exploit a processor's ability to execute instructions speculatively—predicting what code should run without certainty—and then leak secret information through timing side channels. Finding these bugs is hard because existing fuzzers (automated testing tools) can't reliably set up the exact microarchitectural state needed to trigger these vulnerabilities, nor can they detect when secret data leaks. DejaVuzz introduces two new techniques: Dynamic Swappable Memory (DSM), which swaps physical memory pages at runtime to precisely control the state of the processor's caches, address translation buffers, and branch predictor; and Differential Information Flow Tracking (DIFT), which instruments the processor simulator to detect when secret data flows to an observable channel (like cache timing). Together, these enable both broad coverage testing and precise detection of information leakage.
